US guidelines allow for 5 years of letrozole after a full course of tamoxifen.3 The rel- ative efficacy of the different aromatase inhibitors availa- ble (and whether steroidal and nonsteroidal inhibitors vary in their effects and could beneficially be combined) is also under investigation.31 Aromatase inhibitors are not effective for hormonal thera- py in premenopausal women with ER-positive disease,3 although combination of ovarian suppression with a gona- dorelin analogue (or ovarian ablation by surgery or irradi- ation) and aromatase inhibitor therapy is being studied.37 The optimum sequencing of surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy/hormonal therapy continues to be investi- gated. Concurrent chemo- and radiotherapy is not feasible with current regimens because of toxicity; on the basis of limited data,38,39 radiotherapy given after chemotherapy is preferred,3 as it appears to be more effective. Whether tamoxifen should be given concurrently or sequentially with radiotherapy remains unclear, despite several studies addressing the question.39 Where both chemotherapy and hormonal therapy are given, it is recommended that chem- otherapy should precede hormonal therapy.3 The use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy before surgery in locally ad- vanced disease (see below) has led to its investigation in early disease. While studies have shown its use allows an increase in breast-conserving surgery, there is no clear ev- idence of an improvement in disease-free or overall sur- vival.40 In locally advanced breast cancer (stage III) the few pa- tients for whom initial surgery is feasible may be treated as those with high-risk early breast cancer (see above). How- ever, most patients begin with anthracycline-based neoad- juvant chemotherapy, which usually results in sufficient tumour shrinkage to allow surgical management, as well as allowing assessment of the responsiveness of the tu- mour to subsequent treatment.3,8 Radiotherapy and adju- vant chemotherapy are used after surgery, and tamoxifen is also added if the disease is oestrogen-receptor positive.3 The aims of therapy in advanced disease (stage IV) are palliation and prolongation of life; cure is generally not possible with current regimens,1,3 and it is often appropri- ate to select therapy on the basis of its adverse effects, to achieve optimal risk/benefit ratios.41 In women with ER- positive, limited, or asymptomatic disease, hormonal ther- apy is preferred: US guidelines advocate an aromatase in- hibitor (anastrozole, letrozole, or exemestane), or an anti- oestrogen (usually tamoxifen) for first-line hormonal ther- apy in postmenopausal patients; second-line therapy op- tions include fulvestrant, toremifene, progestogens such as megestrol, andro
